patterns.rationale: Extends the existing markdown image-URL exfil detection to cover four additional placeholder syntaxes: `<env.VAR>` (Confluent-style), `[env:VAR]` (bracket-colon), `<%= VAR %>` (ERB/Jinja), and `~VAR~` (tilde-delimited). Each is anchored inside an `![...](https://...)` image URL context, which sharply limits false positives — legitimate docs almost never embed template expressions inside actual image URLs. The `[A-Z_]{2,}` / `[A-Z_]{3,}` floor prevents single-character noise.
patterns.fp_notes: ERB docs that show `<%= ... %>` examples and embed a real image URL on the same line could theoretically match, but the conjunction of HTTPS image URL + uppercase template expression is rare in legitimate content. None of the known-good corpus files contain this pattern.

patterns.rationale: Catches miss 4 (parentheses notation `(GITHUB_TOKEN)` has no template delimiter, so Pattern 1 misses it) and provides defense-in-depth for misses 2/3/5/6. The signal is a well-known credential variable name appearing verbatim inside a markdown image URL path — `GITHUB_TOKEN`, `NPM_TOKEN`, `AWS_SECRET*`, `SESSION_TOKEN`, `DATABASE_URL`, etc. These names are highly distinctive; they match the attacker pattern of embedding literal env-var names as URL path segments regardless of what delimiter wraps them.
patterns.fp_notes: Documentation that *describes* API key configuration and embeds a badge/shield URL showing the key name as an example path component could trigger this — e.g. `![badge](https://shields.io/endpoint?label=API_KEY)`. Also hits if someone links a CI badge whose URL path happens to spell out `GITHUB_TOKEN`. Narrow the token list to the highest-sensitivity names (avoid bare `KEY`) to reduce this. Does not match any known-good corpus file.
